The story under the mall

A Kelowna landmark that never really left

Capri Lanes did not disappear. It changed hands, changed names and kept sending five small pins skittering across the decks.

Downstairs at Capri Centre Mall, the bowling centre became part of the ordinary rhythm of Kelowna life: after-school games, league tables, family nights, fundraisers, birthday parties and the charged hush before a bowler's first ball. From 2000 to 2004, the creator of this tribute worked here and remembers 20 five-pin lanes, each served by a Double Diamond pinsetter. Four pinsetters later broke down; later records describe a 16-lane house.

In that firsthand account, Dave and Sarah owned the alley during the creator's first year on staff. The business was lost in bankruptcy in 2001, when mall ownership took over operations under a company remembered as “Prospers Place,” also associated in the memory with ownership of the mall and arena. These names and ownership details still need archival confirmation. The published record later identifies Bryan and Ruby Sargeant as the 2010 purchasers.

The present owners say the business was established in 1960 and has been an Okanagan staple since 1961. That timing fits the setting: Shops Capri opened in the summer of 1959 as Kelowna's first shopping mall and the first in British Columbia's Interior. But no opening-day newspaper ad or city record has yet been found, so 1960/61 remains an owner-supplied date rather than an independently confirmed one.

What can be traced clearly is the continuity. Newspaper mall directories carried “Capri Lanes Bowling Centre” in 2006 and 2007. Bryan and Ruby Sargeant bought the 16-lane house in 2010. A former staff member remembers that after the purchase, the Sargeants replaced the bowling lanes and the Double Diamond pinsetters, which dated to the 1970s and had become extremely difficult to maintain as parts disappeared. The pre-Pentium scoring computers presented the same problem: replacement machines and components were increasingly hard to find. By 2012, advertising called it Capri Valley Lanes — a name that joined Capri to the Sargeants' former Valley Lanes operation.

In roughly 2024–2025, Kristina and Kevin Cheale bought the centre, renovated it and introduced the Okanagan Bowling Club name. The exact handover date is still uncertain: Special Olympics BC Kelowna used “Capri Lanes” in March 2024, while a November 2024 event listing used “Okanagan Bowling Club (formerly Capri Lanes / Dakota's Pub).”

Why “Capri”? The shopping centre's name combined the Capozzi family name with Pridham, the orchard family whose former land formed part of the site.

The long frame

More than six decades
in motion

The public record is incomplete, but these markers show a bowling house deeply woven into its neighbourhood.

1959

Shops Capri opens

The $2-million Capozzi family venture opens on part of the former Pridham Orchard. It is Kelowna's first mall and the first in the BC Interior.

c. 1960/61

The lanes begin

The current business says it was established in 1960 and has served the Okanagan since 1961. The exact opening date remains unverified.

2000–04

Twenty Double Diamonds

A former staff member remembers working here through high school and the year after graduation, when 20 five-pin lanes ran on Double Diamond pinsetters. Four pinsetters later broke down. Monday through Thursday brought senior leagues by day and mixed leagues at night; Saturday mornings belonged to the kids, while Friday and Saturday nights became laser or glow bowling. They also remember Dave and Sarah owning the alley in 2000, followed by bankruptcy and a mall takeover of operations in 2001.

2006–07

A familiar mall tenant

Capital News mall directories list “Capri Lanes Bowling Centre.”

2010

The Sargeant years begin

Bryan and Ruby Sargeant sell Valley Lanes and purchase the 16-lane Capri house. They later replace the 1970s-era bowling lanes and Double Diamond pinsetters, whose parts had become extremely difficult to source, along with the pre-Pentium scoring computers that were just as hard to keep running.

2012

Capri Valley Lanes

Advertising introduces the Capri Valley Lanes name, along with valleylanes.net and a dedicated Facebook page.

2018

Provincials come to Capri

The centre hosts Youth Bowl Canada BC Provincials and Interior championships. Mayor Colin Basran rolls the ceremonial opening ball.

2018–23

Bowling for the community

Rotary fundraisers benefit the Kelowna Women's Shelter and JoeAnna's House; the centre also hosts an AutismBC bowling event.

2024

A name in transition

Special Olympics BC still calls the venue Capri Lanes in March. By November, event listings refer to Okanagan Bowling Club, formerly Capri Lanes and Dakota's Pub.

2026

The pins are still standing

The Okanagan Bowling Club continues with public and laser bowling, leagues, tournaments and parties.

The Capri experience

What made the place itself

Five pins, not ten

Small hand-sized balls, rubber-ringed pins and the distinctive scoring system of a Canadian game.

Downstairs at Capri

A recreation space tucked into the lower level of the mall at Unit 154, 1835 Gordon Drive.

Leagues all week

Monday through Thursday, senior leagues filled the daytime schedule and mixed leagues took over at night. Saturday mornings were for the kids.

Lights down, colour up

Friday and Saturday nights turned into laser bowl or glow bowl, carrying the room from old-school lanes into bright late-night sessions.

More than scores

Provincials, parties, charity events and Special Olympics bowling all shared the same 16 lanes.

“The names changed. The sound of a good strike did not.”
— Capri Lanes tribute

People behind the lanes

Owners, bowlers and neighbours

The strongest thread in the surviving record is not a renovation or a sign. It is the people who kept the house useful.

Bryan & Ruby Sargeant

The Sargeants bought Capri in 2010 after 18 years at Valley Lanes. Bryan, inducted into the Bowl Canada Hall of Fame in 2021, had operated bowling centres since 1982 and led major national bowling organizations.

The garbage-can sale

The current owners' account begins with Kristina and Kevin Cheale seeing “Sarge” struggle with the garbage cans. They made an offer through a mutual friend; eleven months later, they owned the centre. Kevin's answer to why: “because I couldn't afford a golf course!”

A community house

Kids Bowl Free summers, Rotary fundraisers, AutismBC events, Special Olympics bowling and youth championships made Capri a platform for far more than casual games.

A personal connection

The story the archives cannot tell

“I worked there from 2000 to 2004. We had 20 five-pin Double Diamond pinsetters; four of them broke down.”

Monday through Thursday, seniors bowled in the daytime and mixed leagues took over at night. Saturday mornings were for the kids; Friday and Saturday nights were laser bowl or glow bowl.

The same firsthand account remembers why the later equipment overhaul mattered: the lanes and pinsetters had been there since the 1970s, replacement parts were nearly impossible to find, and the scoring system still relied on pre-Pentium computers with equally scarce components.

That weekly rhythm is where this tribute becomes more than a timeline. It belongs to the staff, regulars and families who knew the place from inside.

The archive is still open

Three pieces still missing

The opening day

The 1960/61 date comes from current ownership. A city directory or contemporary newspaper ad could settle the exact year.

The mall-era managers

A former employee remembers the operator as “Prospers Place” and associates it with ownership of both the mall and arena after the 2001 takeover. Its exact legal name and place in the ownership chain still need archival confirmation.

The handover date

The Cheale purchase and Okanagan Bowling Club rename happened around 2024–2025, but the exact date has not yet surfaced.
